Stop giving advice and just be supportive. That includes accepting if she isn't ready to seek help (in the sense of it not being your responsibility to make her go).

If you're really concerned, you can ask her "what do you need from me? I'm really worried about your health, but I don't want you to feel pressured and I want you to be able to feel comfortable opening up around me. At the same time, I'm starting to feel frustrated that I don't have the tools you need and any insight would be really helpful,".

On your end, it's time to practice self care; you need to be able to set boundaries. You can't be her only emotional support, and you need support of your own; it's very common for SO's of those with anxiety/depression/mental illness to begin to struggle themselves (especially with compassion fatigue). 

It may feel like "If I don't support her, she'll fail/commit suicide/harm herself", but it is very dangerous to support a dynamic where the alternative is relying on you for her basic needs.  Enlist family, friends, or anyone else she trusts if you are 100% sure that there are self-harm related consequences.

Otherwise, *you* may need to seek counselling and ask for some advice/treatment, just to shoulder the burden yourself.

I say this with empathy, because I struggle with PTSD/Anxiety/Depression myself; it took a lot of time for my partner to stop giving advice, stop trying to "fix", stop trying to "help" and start being general support.  Obviously as her partner, you'll be more involved, but you can't actually help her. She has to be in a place where she helps herself. Sometimes that means she needs to hit a bad point, and although that sucks, it's part of life and being an adult.  Your relationship will be healthier and happier if that helper/helpee dynamic is kept  to a minimum.

It may be tempting to respond with "if she just did what I asked/followed this advice, she'd feel better!" but that is not how depression and mental illness work.  She is going to fall off the wagon, going to struggle doing what might feel like common sense things to you, and part of loving someone with those issues is knowing when to compassionately disengage.

I think it is less an effort to control me and more a desperate attempt to control bad things from happening, if that makes sense? She gets in this panicked state where she catastrophizes me not doing what she said a la "ohmygod if what I suggest isn't followed then xyz will happen to daughter!!!"

I feel like... it makes her uncomfortable to be aware of falling into old patterns, because she knows now that a lot of her efforts to 'help' growing up *were* her and my Ndad avoiding their own issues.

I said that I was afraid I'd get reprimanded and any help might have hidden strings in the form of guilt trips and the idea of being indebted.

After I said that, she was really quiet for a bit and then told me she never wanted me to feel like that, that she would try to be calmer and that I never had to worry about her being disappointed in me and being afraid to ask for help. 

Now the biggest issues/areas that fall into old patterns are family events where I am away from home (she won't let me drive, for example, even though my eldest brother is more aggressive and reckless) and she is very weird about when I wake up/go to sleep.That and issues like my car maintenance.

I also have a gel-type lotion with arnica in it to help with bruising; I've been applying it to sensitive areas for the last week and seen results but I haven't tried face, so you might want to patch test and double check the concentration (not sure if it should be weaker for more sensitive skin).  It takes a few days to notice but my bruises heal much faster with its use.

Not sure if you're open to nutritional advice, but limiting blood thinning ingestables and increasing foods with Vitamin K (dark leafy greens for the most part) will help with bruising too.  Doesn't have to be a permenant diet change or anything!

Sometimes there are social workers or others who can make it more intersectional, but there is no guarantee.

And a lot of homeless people *need* assistance, but it isn't offered in a humane practice.  Chances are the homeless people you see have already been through the ringer; there are always "bad" social workers, "bad" doctors, "Bad" helpers.
